name: Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior Detection
description: Methods, tools and empirical studies for detecting coordinated link-sharing and inauthentic network activity on social platforms, from the CooRnet/CLSB methodology to the VERA-AI Alert monitoring system. This is the researcher's signature methodological contribution and remains his most active current research line.

name: Disinformation Narrative Monitoring
description: Tracking and characterizing the spread of disinformation narratives across Europe (e.g. war in Ukraine, LGBTQI+ rights, elections) through language models, dashboards and educational resources for fact-checkers, developed within the PROMPT project and related information operations case studies.

name: Platform Data Access & Research Infrastructure
description: The evolving landscape of researcher access to social media data and APIs under the Digital Service Act, the consequences of CrowdTangle's shutdown, Meta's URL Shares Dataset thresholds, and the researcher's role as a DSA/ECAT independent expert overseeing platform data-access requests.

name: Political Communication & Elections
description: Empirical studies of political news coverage, partisan attention, hyperpartisan networks and polarization dynamics around national and European elections (Italy, Germany, Brazil), a long-running core strand of the MINE programme.

name: Generative AI & Synthetic Media in Disinformation
description: Investigation of how generative AI is used to produce persuasive or deceptive content (e.g. AI-generated gambling promotion imagery, synthetic information operations) and how LLMs can be integrated into research pipelines for political discourse and content classification; also reflected in the researcher's new teaching on generative AI and media.

name: Health Misinformation & Fact-Checking
description: Mapping coordinated networks that circulate problematic health information (COVID-19, vaccine and pandemic-related content) in Italy, India and Nigeria, and building workflows to speed up fact-checking of nefarious actors.

name: Platform Governance & Content Moderation
description: Analysis of platform policy interventions—Meta's political content reduction policy, algorithmic curation of news feeds, and the shift from open to walled-garden platform ecosystems—and their measurable effects on visibility and public debate, including work that has drawn policy and media attention.

name: Computational & LLM-Assisted Content Analysis
description: Methodological work on applying large language models, embeddings and human-in-the-loop pipelines to classify and annotate political and media content at scale, addressing validity, disagreement and reliability challenges in communication research.

name: Social Media Research Methods & Ethics
description: Reflections on the affordances, limits and ethical implications of using social media platforms (Facebook, Twitter/X) as data sources for social science, including survey recruitment via ad platforms and interdisciplinary research ethics—an enduring methodological throughline underpinning the researcher's empirical work.

name: Platforms, Audiences, and Online Communities
description: Empirical and reflective studies of how platform affordances, cultures, and audience practices shape online sociality, identity, and community formation across sites like Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, Twitter/Mastodon, and LiveJournal.

name: Critical Analysis of AI Industry Imaginaries and Discourse
description: Studies examining how AI industry actors, media, and communities construct and circulate narratives, imaginaries, and framings (e.g., longtermism, techno-hagiography, 'quiet futuring', political-economy 'decoys') that shape public understanding and obscure or legitimize the underlying power structures of AI development.

name: Reflections on the State of Misinformation and Online Harm Research
description: Papers that step back from primary empirical study to critically assess the misinformation/online-harms research field itself — diagnosing biases (e.g., WEIRD-centrism, overreliance on cognitive proxies), mapping gaps in evidence (causal, longitudinal, cross-national), and proposing directions or borrowed lessons (e.g., from climate psychology) to make the field more rigorous and generalizable.

name: Theorizing AI's Social Role: Agency, Trust, and Public Perception
description: Papers that apply or extend social theory and communication-trust frameworks to understand the societal position of AI systems, ranging from conceptual demarcations of machine agency and formal multi-agent social frameworks to models of public trust in generative AI and empirical survey data on public attitudes toward AI adoption.

name: Computational Studies of Political Media and Advertising
description: Papers using large-scale computational or quasi-experimental methods to study political advertising, media capture, and ideological signaling on digital platforms, including causal analysis of ad effects, detection of covert advertiser influence on news coverage, and latent ideology estimation of political video content.
